Claremont Attacks/ Hand reattached

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Cape Town is the most sought after destination in the world. Recently It's just been assessed as the 9th most dangerous in the world. Violent crime is on the increase in both poor and affluent areas. Ask Zander Vermeulen who was attacked by a panga-wielding maniac walking away from the notorious Tiger Tiger club in Claremont. His remarkable story of how he was attacked and how a plastic surgeon managed to re-attach his hand will be the main case-study. The attack was so brutal and seemingly senseless that we must ask the question whether this could have been a gang initiation? However it is more likely to be the case of vulnerable club revellers being randomly attacked as they leave the premises. We have video footage of one young women who was brutally attacked last year and we can speak to her and also the brother of a man who was beaten by fellow club goers. We need to ask the club to what extent they are concerned and is it their duty to step up security for patrons.

Press Release:


Hand Reattached
Walking away from a nightclub, young Zander Vermeulen was attacked by a panga-wielding assailant who hacked his hand so badly that it hung by a strand of flesh. The attack was brutal and senseless, raising suspicions that the motive might be linked to gang initiation rites. But through emergency surgery, doctors managed to reattach his severed hand. Can modern surgical techniques restore its functionality completely? Carte Blanche follows his journey to recovery.


Script:


Central Claremont, in Cape Town, becomes a hive of activity at night as students let their hair down at a cluster of nightclubs…. but are they safe?

LINK: While crime has decreased in the Claremont CBD over the past 15 years, there is a sense that attacks have increased in this part of the suburb with criminals targeting revelers as they leave a string of nightclubs.

Once venue Tiger Tiger uses ex club goers, called club watch, to help insure the safety of revelers

Shaun Lewis: They work in association with the local police and CDIC and they firstly patrol inside the clubs and outside in the parking lots and in the road,

But potential danger often lurks for clubbers making their way home. On the 22nd of January 19-year-old student Zander vermeulen was walking home alone early in the morning after visiting two clubs

A car carrying two passengers pulled up on the opposite side of the road, one called over to him

Zander: A man rolled down the window, the window came down and asked me where ABSA main road was, at which point I told him you go to the second robot, you turn left and continued walking.
.
Thinking nothing more of it, zander carried on towards his home.

Zander: There was a shout and I turned to look back and the man was getting out of the car waving a large Panga knife at me.

Horrified, he tried to run away.

Zander: Over here he hit me on the back of the head at which point I fell to my knees. When I looked up he was in front of me.
John: Was he saying anything while he was doing this?
Zander: Nothing, it is quite possible that with the shock I forgot but I remember nothing.

As he got up he did his best to try and defend himself.

Zander: He tried to strike me again with the panga. I raised my left hand and it was severed.

Neighbors heard the commotion and started shouting out. His attacker was startled it seems and Zander ran for his life.

John: I know it is a gory detail but as you were running away during the attack, were you holding your hand in place?
Zander: When I started running I felt it for lack of a better word flapping around and then I held it with my other hand.

He ran back to his flat and from the road screamed foe his housemate Taylor.

Tayler: We heard him come back and he started shouting Tayler, tayler I need to get to a hospital, they have cut off my hand. Then I went and tried to stop the bleeding in his hand. At that point we didn’t actually know how serious it was. We just saw blood everywhere.

She and a friend rushed Zander to a nearby hospital.

Tayler: And in the car her kept counting, he tried to keep conscious. There was a point where, cause obviously he had lost so much blood, that we didn’t really know whether he was going to be okay or not.

LINK: That Zander survived his ordeal was down to a number of factors, all of which fell into place fairly quickly after the attack. One of those is that the assault took place close to the Kingsbury hospital.

Zander was stabilized and then an urgent call was made to plastic and reconstruction surgeon Kevin Adams.

Dr. Adams: I got a call just after 3 o clock on the Friday morning. At that stage of the morning I was a little but sleepy but I woke up quite quickly.

Especially when he heard about the extent of the zander’s injuries from an on duty surgeon.

Dr Adams: he said the hand has been completely severed apart from a small bridge of skin and I said are any bones still connected and he said no

Dr Adams got onto phone to call together a surgical team. And then headed for the Kingsbury. Back at the hospital the news was not looking good.

John: What was your reaction when they said that they might lose your hand?
Zander: Well I already knew that there was a very strong possibility the second I saw it had been severed so I already had made peace with the fact.

Zander has a deep gash to his skull, which could be easily treated. It was his hand that dr Adams and his team were desperate to save. What was in Zander’s favor was that the weapon used was extremely sharp.

Dr Adams: one of the good things about that is that if you cut through a blood vessel with something sharp, a faulty straight cut, and it allows the vessel to then go into spasm and stop the bleeding so he wasn’t actively bleeding by the time we started the operation
John: How technical was the operation?
Dr Adams: So the first operation we did was about 3 and a half hours or so but that was focusing on the primary objective which was to stabilize the bones and the reconnect the blood vessels so that blood would be able to get in and blood would be able to drain out of the rest of the hand and that essentially is what was going to determine whether it stayed alive or not.

Here you can see the steel pins the team used to stabilize and hold the bones of his hand together. .

At about seven in the morning zander was taken through to ICU and monitored. The team carried on with their workday before returning later that evening.

John: What did part 2 of the surgery involve?
Dr Adams': Part 2 was cleaning out all the blood clots

And then over the next 5 hours the delicate task – the reconnection of the four main nerves, the tendons and the muscles.

While the operation was taking place, Zander’s father was in the air.

John: As a parent myself I can't imagine getting the kind of call that you did, how did you respond in that moment?
Chris: Well it is a call no parent ever wants to get and I was in France, my wife called me and 3 o’clock in the morning so I had to rush back so you can imagine my wife. The position she was in, she had to deal with it all on her own.

After landing in Cape Town he got to the Kingsbury as quickly as possible.

Chris: When I saw my son I realized he was fine. It was just a huge relief.


Zanders was discharged after only 5 days – but the road is long and uncertain – he needs intensive occupational and physiotherapy Only time will tell whether he will regain full use of his hand.

Dr. Adams: in the next little while we will be waiting to see how well the nerves regenerate and again part of the integral function of the hand is to be able to feel what you are doing because otherwise it is a bit like a paper weigh. The most we would hope for is protective sensation, anything more than that that we get would be ideal
Zander: So far I am not allowed to move my hands or my fingers cause that could snap the tendons. I have several bolts running through it to stop me from moving it but everything is looking good so far the doctors say.

LINK: The brutality of the attack on Zander has baffled his family friends and even the police. The question on all of their lips, what could possibly have motivated it?

Zander has no idea, nor does his father.

You know the kids went clubbing the previous evening and I checked with all of them and my first response was, was there any conflict and all of them gave me the assurance that no, nothing of that sort occurred. You think about, you hear these stories of drug-induced frenzies taking place and the gang initiation scenario. Robbery, we not sure because he was not robbed, we not sure whether the robbery was foiled by the screaming of witnesses and stuff. And then one wonders whether there is some mad person doing the rounds just going around with a machete and just getting some satisfaction out of hurting people. I don’t know, its a, time will tell.

Abdul parker heads up the local Claremont CID. He put the question of gang initiation to the detective in charge.

Abdul: I haven’t seen it in my experience and I have also been around the block a few times. He is the head of detectives. He hasn’t seen it. Not discounting it but haven’t seen it before.

But there have been some terrible assaults recently on patron when they have travelled away from the club, one fatal. Dr. Adams is often faced with the consequence

Dr Adams: I've had numerous patients come from a limited number of clubs in the Claremont area over the last 5 years.
John: What sorts of injuries do you see coming out of these clubs?
Dr Adams: Assaults whether it is assault with a blunt object, sort of fist boots that sort of thing. And again interpersonal attacks.

The management of Tiger Tiger is also concerned about Zanders case.

Anick: Obviously we do see it as tragic but you know we cant, we obviously take the safety of our patrons very seriously but what happens when they leave is often beyond our control.
Shaun: But we try to get together as a community of nightclub venues to try and come up with ways to educate out patrons on the safety around going home alone and walking in the streets at 3 o clock in the morning.



AND THAT’S THE REASON WHY TAYLOR POSTED ZANDER’S STORY ON FACE BOOK AND WAS OVERWHELMED BY THE RESPONSE.

Tayler: My concern, both zander and my concern at that time was just spreading awareness to all of the students because everybody walks home alone, everybody in the street walks home alone and they didn’t know what happened.

John: Looking back on the incident Chris, is there any anger? Are you angry at the levels of violence in this country?
Chris: I think I am no more angry than any other South African. I think obviously you go through stages and then I, we as a family, we trust the police. We have no reason to believe that they are not doing everything in their power to find the culprit.

ZANDER has in the meantime started trauma counseling. He hopes that his story will encourage patrons to be more aware.

Zander: I don’t want people to use what happened to me as an excuse to stop their children from going out or being able to enjoy their life in Claremont or the entire cape town region for that matter but rather to use it as an example and to use preventive measures to make sure it doesn’t happen again. Use social media to tell each other which streets aren’t safe and always keep an eye on each other.
John: Looking back is there anything you would change about that night?
Zander: Taken a different route.
